cells.tense: You notice what another person is carrying, and it stays their weather while you stay yours.
cells.ask: Next time you plan something with someone, say what you actually want before you ask what they want. Then leave a pause and don't fill it.
cells.core:
Someone tells you about their week and you take it in — the tiredness, the worry — without it becoming yours to fix or yours to feel. That's harder than it sounds, and you're doing it. You've found the range where you can be moved by people and still be the one who decides what happens next.

It takes adjusting, though. Some days the read comes quick and you give more than the moment asked; some days you hold back when they wanted you closer. The sense that tells you which is which is the whole skill here, and it runs on contact — on actually saying your side of things instead of quietly matching theirs. That's the door in. One exchange where you name what you want, and you'll feel the difference in your own body within a day or two.
cells.sheetLine: Being moved by someone without disappearing into them.
cells.verb: Feeling with another person while keeping hold of your own shape
cells.place: Where you keep checking the flow — how much to give, how much to hold back, what to blend

cells.tense: You will be bracing for how someone might take it, and you will already be carrying it before they do.
cells.ask: Before you rearrange your day for someone, ask whether they've actually asked. If nothing is coming, keep the day as it is and don't mention it.
cells.core:
You can feel what's coming before anyone says a word — and you're already acting on it. The mood they'll be in, the thing they'll need, the disappointment waiting if you don't move first. So you move first, and by the time the day arrives you're carrying something nobody handed you.

Here's the part that's easy to miss: the read itself isn't wrong. You're picking up real signals. What needs adjusting is when you answer them. The feeling arrives early, so you give early, and there's no room left for what they'd actually choose. Pull one thing back until it's asked for, and you'll find out something you don't learn otherwise — what happens when you let them want it themselves.
cells.sheetLine: You're already paying for a day that hasn't asked anything of you.
cells.verb: Feeling with another person while keeping hold of your own shape

cells.tense: You once learned to keep your own reactions off the table, and you have been standing at that door ever since.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true thing about how your week has actually been — something you'd normally smooth over. You don't have to go deep and they don't have to respond well.
cells.core:
You can talk with anyone and it all stays level — friendly, useful, and about an inch deep. Somewhere along the way being moved by people started costing too much, and the way through was to keep your own reactions out of it. That worked. It also means almost nobody knows what you actually think.

It didn't go anywhere, though. It's the way back in that's out of practice, and it comes back through small honest moments, not big ones. Steady ground here isn't a state you find; it's something you keep re-sensing by letting a little of yourself arrive. That's the door. You don't need to become a person who floods; you need one moment where something real shows through and the room holds it.
cells.sheetLine: The door you're standing at is one you already walked through.

cells.tense: They are already getting the real thing from you, and you are describing it to yourself as not being a person who does that.
cells.ask: Write down one kindness you did this week without noticing you meant it, and say the reason out loud once — to yourself, or to one person who won't make it a thing.
cells.core:
People come to you when they're unsteady. They say you're easy to talk to, that you make room, that you don't flinch — and you hear it as politeness. Meanwhile you'd tell anyone that you're not particularly soft; you just deal with things.

Both are true and only one is the account you're keeping. Whatever it is you do — how you listen, what you don't make into a problem, the way you let people be however they are — is the same instinct, and you've been filing it under logistics. Taking credit isn't vanity here. It's accuracy. Seeing the shape of what you already do is the difference between it running you and you steering it.

The reader could reasonably say 'I'm not numb, I just keep my work life separate,' and the door the core describes should be narrow enough to fit that. The ask survives being wrong because it produces one honest exchange either way, and the sentence that serves me is 'Can't tell where you end and others begin' — it needs softening to the moment.
